_doc: AMZN segments config for emit_segments.py. A BRIDGE is a chain of terms whose product equals a target — that is the generic shape, so Uber's 'GB = MAUs x trips/MAU x price' and AWS's 'revenue = capacity x revenue per $ of capacity' are the same object with different terms. Drivers that already live in js/results-data/amzn.js are REFERENCED (from: results:<key>), never copied, so segment revenue and operating income keep exactly one home.
_shared_note: Drivers Bloomberg reports for the company as a whole, not per segment. RPO is essentially all AWS for Amazon, but that is an assumption and the note says so on screen.
_rejected_note: Checked and deliberately excluded. The DCF's segment D&A is an even three-way split (US, Intl and AWS all read 4809.5188588 in 2026Q2) so it is an allocation, not a measurement — Bloomberg's segment D&A differs by segment and is used instead. The DCF's actuals_history FCF row reads 99,595 for 2026Q2 against CFO 45,387 + capex -54,208 = -8,821, so it is on some other definition and is not read. Bloomberg's inventory turnover is 0.00 in all 30 snapshots.

segments.label: AWS
segments.lede: The profit engine, and the reason the capex line looks the way it does. AWS sells compute, storage and managed services on capacity Amazon has to build before it can sell it — so the honest read is not price x units, it is contracted demand against deployed capacity.

sells.name: Compute
sells.what: EC2 instances and the managed layers on top of them; increasingly accelerated instances for training and inference.

sells.name: Storage & data
sells.what: S3, EBS, and the database and analytics services that bill off stored volume and queries.

sells.name: AI platform
sells.what: Bedrock, SageMaker and the Trainium/Inferentia silicon — the newest line and the one driving the capex step-up.

sells.name: Networking & the long tail
sells.what: Data transfer, edge, security and the rest of the managed-service catalogue.

bridges.label: Capacity
bridges.identity: revenue = capacity deployed x revenue per $ of capacity
bridges.note: A decomposition, not an independent build: revenue per $ of capacity IS revenue divided by capacity, so the two terms multiply back to revenue by construction. What it buys you is the split — how much of the revenue line is more capacity versus better yield on it. Both terms are projected by the model, so the split runs forward.

bridges.label: Backlog
bridges.identity: revenue = contracted backlog x conversion into the quarter
bridges.note: Bloomberg reports remaining performance obligations for the company; for Amazon that is essentially all AWS, which is an assumption worth holding lightly. Backlog is the closest thing AWS has to a units number — demand already signed and not yet delivered.

segments.label: North America
segments.lede: The retail surface at home: first-party stores, the third-party marketplace riding the same fulfilment network, and advertising riding on both. Amazon discloses no units, no average selling price and no Prime member count, so a classic price x quantity bridge cannot be built honestly here.

sells.name: Online stores (1P)
sells.what: Amazon's own inventory, sold and shipped by Amazon.

sells.name: Third-party seller services
sells.what: Commissions, FBA fulfilment and shipping fees from sellers on the same network.

sells.name: Advertising
sells.what: Sponsored placement against shopping intent — reported company-wide, not split by segment.

sells.name: Subscriptions & physical stores
sells.what: Prime and content subscriptions; Whole Foods, Fresh and Go.

bridges.label: Capacity
bridges.identity: revenue = fulfilment capacity x revenue per $ of capacity
bridges.note: The only bridge the disclosure supports for retail. Read it as network productivity — and read it against AWS, because the gap between the two is the whole difference between the businesses in one number.

segments.label: International
segments.lede: The same retail model outside North America, several years behind on margin and with a different mix of owned versus marketplace. Same disclosure limits as North America.

sells.name: Online stores (1P)
sells.what: Amazon's own inventory in each country it operates.

sells.name: Third-party seller services
sells.what: The marketplace, at a lower share of the mix than North America.

bridges.label: Capacity
bridges.identity: revenue = fulfilment capacity x revenue per $ of capacity
bridges.note: International carries the least owned infrastructure per dollar sold of the three segments. That reads as high productivity and is really a mix statement: more of the sales here run through the marketplace and through leased rather than owned capacity.

_derived_note: Ratios the generator computes from two drivers. `annualiseDen` multiplies the denominator by the periods-per-year of the view, so a quarterly coverage ratio reads against a run-rate rather than against a single quarter.
_highlights_note: Per segment, the derived ratios worth putting on screen beside the bridge.
